Stiff-man syndrome: identification of 17 h-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase
type 4 as a novel 80-kDa antineuronal antigen
Klaus Dinkel a, Mathias Rickert a, Gabriele Mo¨ller b, Jerzy Adamski b,
Hans-Michael Meinck c, Wiltrud Richter a,*
aDepartment of Orthopedic Surgery, University of Heidelberg, Schlierbacher Landstr . 200, 69118 Heidelberg, Germany
bInstitute for Experimental Genetics, GSF-National Research Center of Environment and Health, P .O. 1129, 85758 Neuherberg, Germany
cDepartment of Neurology, University of Heidelberg, Im Neuenheimer Feld, 69120 Heidelberg, Germany
Received 10 April 2001; received in revised form 19 June 2002; accepted 20 June 2002
Abstract
Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) is a rare autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system associated with autoantibodies to glutamate
decarboxylase (GAD). We isolated five brain-reactive human monoclonal antibodies, with reactivity distinct from GAD, from peripheral
blood of a patient newly diagnosed with SMS. Two antibodies reacted with both Purkinje cells and ependymal cells, and precipitated an 80-
kDa protein from rat neuronal primary cultures, which was also recognized by 12% (3/25) of SMS sera and 13% (2/15) of SMS cerebrospinal
fluid (CSF) samples. The corresponding antigen was identified as 17 h-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 4 and may represent a possible
novel target of autoimmunity in SMS.

Keywords: Human monoclonal antibodies; Autoimmune disease; Mass spectrometry
1. Introduction
Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) and its variants are rare
disorders of the central nervous system characterized by
progressive muscle rigidity and superimposed painful
spasms (Moersch and Woltman, 1956). Stiffness and spasms
are thought to result from a dysfunction of inhibitory g-
aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic neuronal pathways
(Meinck et al., 1994) . In addition to these two obligatory
symptoms, patients may develop a variety of facultative
neurological or psychiatric symptoms such as ataxia, retin-
opathy or agoraphobia (Barker et al., 1998; Brown and
Marsden, 1999; Henningsen et al., 1996; Tinsley et al.,
1997). The etiology and pathogenesis of SMS and its
variants are unknown. However, since these disorders are
frequently associated with other autoimmune diseases like
type I diabetes mellitus (Bosi et al., 1988; Solimena et al.,
1988), an autoimmune hypothesis was suggested for SMS
(Blum and Jankovic, 1991; Young, 1966) . Supporting this
hypothesis, autoantibodies directed against the GABA-syn-
thesizing enzyme, glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD),
were identified in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
of 60 – 80% of SMS patients (Solimena et al., 1988, 1990) .
GAD-autoantibody-positive sera from SMS patients can
inhibit GABA synthesis in vitro (Dinkel et al., 1998) ,
suggesting that GAD antibodies may have an implication
in GABAergic dysfunction. In SMS patients associated with
breast cancer, autoantibodies to the 128-kDa protein amphi-
physin occur in the absence of GAD antibodies (Folli et al.,
1993). One patient with clinical features of SMS and media-
stinal cancer showed antibodies directed to gephyrin, a cy-
tosolic protein concentrated at the postsynaptic membrane
of inhibitory synapses. In three other patients without asso-
ciated tumors, antibodies to an unknown 80-kDa antigen have
been reported (Darnell et al., 1993; Horiuchi et al., 1998) .
In this study, we set out to further characterize the

humoral immune response in patients with SMS in order
to identify additional SMS-associated autoantigens and
possible target cells in the nervous system. We screened
the B cell repertoire from a patient newly diagnosed with
SMS for IgG-secreting B cells with reactivity to brain

antigens and report about the isolation of four human
monoclonal B cell lines with reactivities distinct from

2. Patients and methods
2.1. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid
Samples of serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were
obtained with informed consent. Peripheral blood mononu-
clear cells were obtained from a patient, HG (female, 62
years), at diagnosis of SMS. By then, the patient experi-
enced painful spasms and stiffness in her right leg since 5
years. Spasms were associated with agoraphobia, falls,
hyperhidrosis and tachycardia. Two years later, spasms
and stiffness involved also the left leg and the trunk. In
1993, SMS was diagnosed on the basis of typical clinical
and electromyographic (EMG) findings, presence of auto-
antibodies against both GAD and thyroidal microsomes, and
normal cranial and thoracic magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI). In the following years, she developed vertigo and
positional nystagmus (1994), gait ataxia and diabetes melli-
tus (1995), limb ataxia, mild dementia and multiple white
matter enhancements on repeat cranial MRI (1997), dys-
arthria (1998), and insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus
(IDDM, 1999).
Serum samples were collected from 25 SMS patients
diagnosed according to previously described criteria
(Meinck et al., 1994; Gordon et al., 1967; Lorish et al.,
1989; Moersch and Woltman, 1956) Serum samples from
healthy blood donors ( n = 15) were used as controls. CSF
was available from 15 SMS patients and from 10 patients
with other (non-autoimmune) neurological disorders (OND).
2.2. Production and cloning of human monoclonal B cell
lines
B cells from peripheral blood of the GAD-antibody-
positive patient HG were isolated and immortalized with
Epstein – Barr virus as described before (Richter et al.,
1989). IgG-producing cells were selected using anti-IgG-
coated magnetic beads (Dynal) and cultured in microtiter
plates for several weeks as described (Richter et al., 1992) .
Culture supernatants were screened for their reactivity with
sections of rat cerebellar cortex by indirect immunohisto-
chemistry. Reactive B cell lines were expanded and cloned
repeatedly on a single cell level for stabilization of IgG
production (Richter et al., 1992) . Some lines were fused
with the human – mouse heteromyeloma cell line SHM-D33
(A TCC# CRL-1668) prior to cloning. Human monoclonal B
cell lines were maintained in Iscove’s modified Dulbeccos
medium (Gibco) supplemented with 15% fetal calf serum
(FCS, Seromed), 2 mM glutamine (Gibco), 100 U/ml
penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco), insulin and oxalacetate,
and cell supernatants used as a source for antibody studies.
2.3. Immunohistochemistry
Rats were killed by intraperitoneal injection of an excess
amount of sodiumpentobarbital (200 mg/kg body weight)
The brains were immediately removed and snap-frozen. Five-
micrometer-thick sections were cut in a cryostat at /C018 jC,
dried and stored at /C080 jC. Cerebellar primary cultures
grown on coverslips were fixed with acetone/PBS (50:50) for
5 min at /C020 jC. Specimen were incubated for 1 h in a moist
chamber with either 30 Al (cerebellum sections) or 60 Al
(coronal sections of hemispheres) of culture supernatant from
B cell lines. Iscove’s medium was used as a negative control.
Sections were washed three times with phosphate-buffered
saline (PBS) for 5 min, incubated with a fluorescence-
diacetate-conjugated anti-human IgG (Dianova; 1:200 in
PBS, 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA), 1 h, 20 jC) or

horseradish peroxidase-conjugated anti-human IgG antibody
from goat (Dianova; 1:500 in PBS, 3% BSA, 45 min, 37 jC).
The sections were washed three times with PBS for 5 min,
incubated for 5 min with diaminobenzidine (Sigma) as
substrate for peroxidase, dried, mounted and observed under
a light or fluorescent microscope, respectively.
2.4. Striatal and cerebellar primary cultures
Striata/cerebella from Wistar/WAG (Boehringer-Ingel-
heim) day 17 embryos (E17) were dissected under a
binocular microscope and cells were dissociated by incuba-
tion in 0.25% trypsin/EDTA solution (Sigma) for 20 min at
room temperature. The enzyme solution was removed, the
tissue was resuspended in Hanks buffered salt solution
(Gibco) 10% FCS, and dissociated by triturating using an
18-gauge needle. The cell suspension was centrifuged at
800 /C2g for 8 min and the pellet resuspended in minimal
essential medium (MEM, Gibco) 10% horse serum (HS,
Gibco). The total cell number was determined using a
Neubauer chamber. Striatal (200,000 cells/cm
2) and cere-
bellar (100,000 cells/cm 2) cultures were seeded in poly-
ornithine-coated dishes (Sigma). The cerebellar cultures
were maintained for 22 days in MEM 10% HS supple-
mented with high glucose (4.5 mg/ml), 5 Ag/ml insulin and
10 Ag/ml transferrin. The medium was changed every 2 – 3
days. The striatal mixed cultures were maintained in the
same medium for 4 days and then radiolabeled. Ependymal
cell enriched cultures from cerebellum were obtained by a
modified method of Weibel et al. (1986) .
2.5. Radiolabeling of cells and protein extraction
Radiolabeling of striatal mixed primary cultures was
performed after 4 days of culturing. Most of the medium
was removed, and cells were incubated for 45 min at 37 jC
with 5 ml/10 cm dish methionine-free MEM.
35S-methio-
nine (300 ACi/10 cm dish) was added and cells were labeled
for 18 h at 37 jC. Cells were washed three times in ice-cold
Tris-buffered saline (pH 8.0), lysed for 30 min on ice in a

modified RIPA buffer (0.15 M NaCl, 1% NP-40, 1%
deoxycholate, 0.1% sodiumdodecylsulfate, 10 mM sodium
phosphate, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 2 mM EDTA, and 1 tablet/
15 ml of protease inhibitor cocktail (Boehringer Man-
nheim)) and clarified at 29,000 /C2g for 1 h at 4 jC. Extracts
from non-labeled cerebellar cultures were obtained by the
same protocol.
2.6. Immunoprecipitation (IP)
Samples from radiolabeled extracts were standardized to
10
6 cpm/IP . The extracts were incubated on ice overnight
with either 8 Al of serum, 80 Al of CSF or 200 Al of culture
supernatant from B cell lines. Fifty microliters per IP of
swollen protein A Sepharose (PAS, Pharmacia) was added
and incubated for 2 h on ice. Centrifugal washing (300 /C2g,
2 min) of the PAS pellet was done four times with Schwyzer
washing buffer (100 mM Tris/Cl, 500 mM LiCl, 1% Triton
X-100, 1% h-mercaptoethanol, pH 9.0), four times with
PBS and once with pure water. Proteins were resolved on
10% SDS-polyacrylamide gels and detected by autoradiog-
raphy using an intensifying screen at /C070 jC. If serum was
used for IP , the extract was precleared by 4 h incubation on
ice with 8 Al normal human serum and 50 Al of swollen
PAS. After centrifugation (300 /C2g, 2 min), the supernatant
was used for IP with patients’ serum.
2.7. Immunoblotting
After immunoprecipitation of rat cerebellum and rat liver
extracts by adjusted amounts of GF5 or CB11 antibody,
samples were boiled, separated by denaturing 10% SDS gel
electrophoresis and electrophoretically transferred to a nitro-
cellulose membrane (semi-dry Western blotting). Blocking
was performed in 5% BSA in phosphate-buffered saline
(PBS). Membranes were incubated with rabbit anti-17 h-
HSD4-specific antibody KV (1:100), followed by horse-
radish peroxidase-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG antibody
(1:20,000). Bound antibody was visualized on X-ray films
using the chemiluminescent ECL system (ECL, Amersham).
2.8. Purification of the 80-kDa antigen
Large amounts of unlabeled extracts (25 ml/IP) from
cerebellar cultures (20 dishes of 10 cm) were immunopre-
cipitated with 22 ml culture supernatant of CB11 bound to
PAS. After the last washing step, the PAS pellet was
incubated for 45 min at 37 jC with 400 Al of elution buffer
(7 mM Tris/Cl, 1.5% SDS, 1% h-mercaptoethanol, pH 6.8)
to elute the bound proteins. After centrifugation, the super-
natant was collected, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and
lyophilized overnight in a speed vac. Reconstitution was
performed by adding 35 AlH
2O (distilled), 5 Al glycerol and
0.3 mg bromphenol blue. This method was used in order to
concentrate the precipitated antigen in a small volume of
SDS sample buffer.
2.9. Protein sequencing
Concentrated proteins were resolved after IP on a 10%
SDS-polyacrylamide gel and visualized by Coomassie R-
250 (Sigma) staining. Excised gel pieces containing the 80-
kDa protein were carboxymethylated and submitted to
tryptic digestion. The obtained peptide mixture was ana-
lyzed by mass spectrometry (MALDI-MS), and the mass
fingerprint was compared to NCBI database using the
‘‘Profound’’ search algorithm [PROTAGEN (Bochum, Ger-
many)]. Bands above 80 kDa were analyzed by the same
procedure.
2.10. Assay of 17 b-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase
Rat liver was homogenized in PBS/0.1% Brij35 in the
presence of proteinase inhibitor. After centrifugation at
1000 /C2g for 10 min, the supernatant was centrifuged at
100,000 /C2g for 90 min and the resulting supernatant was

filtered (0.45 Am). In parallel, 37 Al PAS was incubated for 1
ha t4 jC with 10 ml of cell culture medium containing
either CB11, a human monoclonal control antibody GF5 or
no antibody at all. After washing, the PAS – antibody com-
plexes were incubated for 2.5 h at 4 jC each with 6 ml of
filtered rat liver extract. The PAS – antibody – antigen com-
plexes were washed five times with PBS/0.1% Brij35 and
finally resuspended in 200 Al of the same buffer. Equal
aliquots of the complexes were taken for enzyme.
For the determination of oxidative 17 h-hydroxysteroid
dehydrogenase (17 h-HSD4) activity, immune complexes
(15 Al) were incubated in 100 mM sodium phosphate

mM NAD + in a final volume of 500 Al. After 35 min at
37 jC, the reaction was stopped by the addition of 100 Alo f
0.21 M ascorbic acid in methanol/acetic acid (99:1). Ste-
roids were extracted on RP-18 cartridges, and the substrate
estradiol was separated from the product estrone by
reversed phase (C18) high performance liquid chromatog-

3H-labeled substances was detected online
by a Berthold LB506D monitor as described (Adamski et
al., 1989) .
2.11. Expression of recombinant 17 b-HSD4 proteins
The coding region of rat 17h-hydroxysteroid dehydrogen-
ase type 4 (r17 h-HSD4) was amplified from rat liver cDNA
by standard PCR using primers containing restriction sites for
cloning (forward primer ( SacI): 5V-TTTGAGCTCGA TGTC-
GCCTCTGAGGTTCGACGG-3V; reverse primer (for full-
length protein r17 h-HSD4(80), XhoI): 5 V-TTTCTCGAGT-
CAGAGCTTGGCA TAGTCTTTCAGAATCA TC-3 V;
reverse primer (for N-terminal domain r17 h-HSD4(32),
Xho I): 5 V-TTTCTCGAGTCA TGA TGCA TCTGCA-

The GST fusion proteins of the 17 h-HSD4 were
expressed in E. coli BL21 DE3 Codon plus (RP) (Strata-

DNA was digested with S. marcescens endonuclease

min centrifugation at 21,000 /C2g.
2.12. Slot-blot
Aliquots of bacteria supernatants containing the same
amount of protein were spotted onto a nitrocellulose
membrane (Schleicher & Schu ¨ll) in a slot-blot device and
air-dried. Blocking was done in 5% powdered milk solution
for 30 min at room temperature. The membranes were
incubated with cell culture supernatants containing either
antibody CB11, antibody GF5 or no antibody at a dilution
of 1:5 with PBS for 16 h at 4 jC. Primary antibody binding
to the proteins was detected by a secondary goat anti-
human IgG antibody (Dianova) coupled to alkaline phos-
phatase. (1:5000, 3 h at room temperature) followed by
staining with Fast Red (Sigma). Alternatively, the mem-
brane was directly incubated with Ponceau red staining
solution.
Fig. 2. Identification of an 80-kDa target antigen. Striatum cells from day
17 (E17) rat embryos were cultured for 4 days and labeled with 35S-
methionine for 18 h. Extracts from this mixed primary cell culture were
immunoprecipitated with the monoclonal antibodies MICA 3 (lane 1), FC2
(lane 4), GG4 (lane 5) and CB11 (lane 6), and subjected to SDS-
polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and autoradiography. Culture medium
was used as a negative control (lanes 2 and 3).
Fig. 3. Reactivity with an 80-kDa antigen in sera and cerebrospinal fluid from SMS patients. (A) 35S-methionine-labeled extracts from striatal mixed primary
cell culture were immunoprecipitated with 8 Al serum from 25 patients with SMS and processed as described in the legend to Fig. 2. The positive samples JF
(lane 1), HG (lane 2) and US (lane 3) are shown together with normal control serum (lane 4) and the CB11-positive control (lane 5). (B) Cerebrospinal flu id
from 15 SMS patients (80 – 100 Al) was used for immunoprecipitation of extracts prepared as in A. Eight SMS-samples are shown, two of which (US, lane 4;
JF, lane 6) react with an 80-kDa protein.

3. Results
3.1. Brain-reactive human monoclonal antibodies derived
from a patient with SMS
Immortalized IgG-positive B cells from peripheral blood
of the patient were screened for their reactivity with cryostat
sections of cerebellum by immunohistochemistry. From 415
oligoclonal cultures, five were positive on cerebellum sec-
tions and four of them could be expanded and stabilized by
repeated cloning on a single cell level. One oligoclonal
GAD-reactive cell line lost reactivity during expansion. The
four stable antibody secreting clones, FC2, GG4, CB7 and
CB11 showed three different staining patterns distinct from
that of GAD antibodies (Fig. 1) . FC2 reacted with the
medulla and the molecular layer (Fig. 1B) and GG4 stained
the medulla (Fig. 1C) . CB7 and CB11 showed reactivity to
the molecular layer and strongly stained Purkinje cells (Fig.
1D). MICA 3, a GAD65-specific antibody derived from a
patient with type I diabetes (Richter et al., 1992) , is shown
for control (Fig. 1A) . According to their staining pattern,
monoclonal antibodies FC2, GG4, CB7 and CB11 recognize
antigens different from GAD. Since CB7 and CB11 revealed
identical staining, only CB11 was used for further studies.
3.2. Recognition of an 80-kDa protein by antibody CB11
The antigens of FC2, GG4 and CB11 were further
characterized using primary cell cultures from embryonic
(E17) rat striatum, which consisted of a mixture of neuronal
and glial cells. Lysates obtained from metabolically labeled
cultures were immunoprecipitated with monoclonal anti-
bodies FC2, GG4, CB11 and MICA 3, respectively. After
separation on a 10% SDS gel, the precipitated proteins were

and cerebellar primary culture cells (d22) enriched for ependymal cells (B) were stained by the human monoclonal antibody CB11. Detection was perfor med by
indirect immunofluorescence (A) or horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies (B). Magnification was 200 /C2.

visualized by autoradiography (Fig. 2) . While monoclonal
antibody CB11 bound to a distinct band at 80 kDa, FC2 and
GG4 failed to precipitate labeled protein from the extracts.
Therefore, FC2 and GG4 were either directed to nonprotein
targets in the brain, or their respective antigen was not present
in the lysates of the cultured primary cells. Since previous
studies had identified SMS sera with an anti-80-kDa protein
reactivity (Darnell et al., 1993; Horiuchi et al., 1998) ,w e
focused on the identification of the 80-kDa CB11 antigen.
3.3. Prevalence of 80-kDa-reactive autoantibodies in SMS
patients
The frequency of 80-kDa antibodies in SMS sera was
determined by immunoprecipitation of extracts from
35S
methionine-labeled primary cultures prepared from rat stria-
tum cells (Fig. 3). Three of the twenty-five (12%) SMS sera
(Fig. 3A) but none of the 15 control sera (not shown)
precipitated a band of 80 kDa. The strong signals of the
80-kDa protein seen with SMS serum from two patients
(Fig. 3A) indicated a high titer of the respective autoanti-
bodies directed to the CB11 autoantigen beside an even
stronger reactivity to GAD as seen by the protein bands
around 65 kDa. A weak anti-80-kDa reactivity occurred in a
third patient in the absence of GAD autoantibodies. In two
of the three patients with anti-80-kDa antibodies in serum,
the CSF was also positive for 80-kDa antibodies (Fig. 3B) .
CSF samples from 13 other SMS patients and from 10
patients with other neurological diseases were negative for
80-kDa antibodies. We conclude that, independent of autor-
eactivity to GAD, 12% of the SMS sera and 13% of the
SMS CSFs reacted with an unknown 80-kDa brain antigen.
3.4. Identification of the 80-kDa antigen as 17 b-hydrox-
ysteroid dehydrogenase type 4
Beside Purkinje cells, cryostat slices from rat cerebellum,
which contained parts of the fourth ventricle, revealed a
strong staining of a distinct cell layer by CB11. In these
epithelial cells, the CB11 antigen was strongly concentrated
towards the lumen of the ventricle (Fig. 4A) . According to
the site and morphology, these cells were considered as
ependymal cells. Using a modified method of Weibel et al.
(1986), we obtained dissociated primary cell cultures from
rat embryonic (E17) cerebellum consisting of 50 – 60%
ependymal cells. This was obvious by the movement of
the cell ciliae in phase contrast microscopy and the reactivity
of monoclonal antibody CB11 with about 50 – 60% of the
cells (Fig. 4B) . Since CB11 did not recognize its antigen in
Western blots (not shown), the 80-kDa antigen was purified
by immunoprecipitation from lysates of the enriched epen-
dymal primary cultures. After immunoprecipitation with
CB11, the proteins were separated on a 10% SDS gel and
then visualized by Coomassie staining (Fig. 5). The 80-kDa
bands and those of higher molecular weight were cut out of
the SDS gel, carboxymethylated, submitted to tryptic diges-
tion and then analyzed by mass spectrometry (MALDI-MS).
After searching the NCBI database, the sequence could be
identified as 17 h-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 4
(17h-HSD4) (probability: 100%). The mass fingerprint cov-
ered 22 – 24% (162 – 176 of 735 amino acids) of the protein.
This enzyme with a molecular weight of 80 kDa is also
named
D-bifunctional peroxisomal protein and plays an
important role in peroxisomal h-oxidation and steroid bio-
synthesis. The bands above 80 kDa represented human IgG 1

(heavy chain) at 97 and 190 kDa and were, thus, derived from
the B cell culture supernatant of the CB11 cell line (Fig. 5).I n
conclusion, we described for the first time that a peroxisomal
protein is a target of human antibodies and demonstrated that
antibodies recognizing 17 h-HSD4 in Purkinje cells occur in
serum and CSF of some individuals with SMS.
3.5. Steroid dehydrogenase enzyme activity precipitated by
CB11
To confirm the identity of the 80-kDa antigen with rat
17h-HSD4, liver extracts were incubated with CB11 bound
to protein A Sepharose. Adjusted amounts of an unrelated
antibody (GF5- or the GAD65-reactive human monoclonal
antibody MICA4) as well as antibody-free medium were
used as a control. Equal amounts of immunoprecipitates
were assayed for enzymatic activity with 17 h-estradiol, the
substrate that is converted by 17 h-HSD4 to estrone. Only
the precipitate of CB11 showed enzymatic activity (Fig.
6A). To confirm expression of 17 h-HSD4 protein in rat
brain and rat liver, native 80-kDA protein was immunopre-
cipitated from rat cerebellum extracts and from rat liver
extracts and subjected to Western blotting. The 80-kDa band

precipitated by CB11 from both extracts was recognized by
a polyclonal rat antiserum directed to 17 h-HSD4 (Fig. 6B) .
3.6. CB11 reacts with recombinant rat 17 b-HSD4
Recombinant r17h-HSD4 was expressed as a GST fusion
protein in E. coli and binding of antibody CB11 was
confirmed by slot-blot analysis. Fig. 6B shows the binding
of CB11 to full-length 17 h-HSD4 from rat, while control
antibody GF5 or cell culture medium were negative. A N-
terminal 32-kDa fragment of 17 h-HSD4 (amino acids 1 –
330) comprising the short-chain alcohol dehydrogenase
(SCAD) domain of 17 h-HSD4 was not recognized by
CB11. The epitope is, therefore, localized at least partially
within amino acids 331 – 735.
4. Discussion
In this study, we screened the peripheral B cell repertoire
of a patient newly diagnosed with SMS and identified five
brain-reactive oligoclonal B cell lines after immortalization
by EBV . One of these cell lines produced antibodies directed
to GAD, whereas four others (FC2, GG4, CB7 and CB11)
recognized different brain antigens according to their stain-
ing pattern on rat cerebellum. An 80-kDa protein was
precipitated by CB7 and CB11 from primary neuronal
cultures of rat striatum. The antigen recognized by CB11
was identified as 17 h-HSD4 by mass spectrometry. Immune
complexes of CB11 with its antigen displayed oxidative
enzymatic activity by converting 17 h-estradiol to estrone
confirming the identity of the 80-kDa CB11 antigen with
17h-HSD4.
Prior reports described a total of three SMS patients with
serum reactivity to an 80-kDa protein of rat and human
cerebellum extracts that had been detected by Western blot-
ting (Darnell et al., 1993; Horiuchi et al., 1998) We confirmed
anti-80-kDa antibodies in about 12% of sera (n = 25) and CSF
samples ( n = 15) of SMS patients by immunoprecipitation.
These patients clinically presented heterogeneously. The
propositus at the time of investigation had SMS and on
follow-ups developed progressive encephalomyelitis with

rigidity and myoclonus, one patient had typical SMS, and the
third patient had paraneoplastic SMS with breast cancer and
antibodies against amphiphysin (Rosin et al., 1998) . Reac-
tivity to the 80-kDa antigen 17 h-HSD4 occurred either
together with GAD reactivity ( n = 2) or without it ( n = 1).
Compared to GAD antibodies, 17 h-HSD4 antibodies, thus,
were less frequent in patients with clinical SMS. Whether the
SMS-associated 80-kDa antibodies described independently
by Darnell et al. (1993) and by Horiuchi et al. (1998)
recognize 17h-HSD4 remains still open.
17h-HSD4 was initially discovered in porcine endome-
trium (Adamski et al., 1992) and shown to be localized in
peroxisomal matrix (Markus et al., 1995) . Its expression in
Purkinje cells and retina has been described before (Normand
et al., 1995) , but its strong polar expression in ependymal
cells had so far not been recognized. Most strikingly, GAD is
also expressed in Purkinje cells and retina and is associated
with synaptic vesicle-like structures localized in the cyto-
plasm (Christgau et al., 1992) . Although 17 h-HSD4 anti-
bodies in CSF would have direct access to the ependymal
cells in vivo, in which the 80-kDa antigen accumulates
towards the lumen of the ventricle, the enzyme will, most
likely, not be directly accessible on the cell surface, a
situation which, again, seems to be similar to GAD.
The orthologue forms of human (Adamski et al., 1995)
and rat 17 h-HSD4 (Corton et al., 1996) have been cloned
and show an identity on the amino acid level of 86% and a
similarity (conservative exchange of amino acids) of 92%.
Mab CB11 reacted with native 17 h-HSD4 from rat liver
extracts and with recombinant rat 17 h-HSD4 expressed as a
GST fusion protein in bacteria. The short-chain alcohol
dehydrogenase (SCAD) domain at the N-terminus of 17 h-
HSD4 alone did, however, not mediate CB11 reactivity
(Fig. 5). Considering previous reports of an SMS-associated
80-kDa autoantigen expressed in rat and in human cerebel-
lum (Darnell et al., 1993; Horiuchi et al., 1998) and the fact
that human monoclonal GAD autoantibodies cross-react
between human, rat and mouse GAD65, we suggest that
human 17 h-HSD4 is an autoantigen addressed in SMS.
17h-HSD4 plays an important role in the steroid inacti-
vation and peroxisomal h-oxidation of fatty acids (de
Launoit and Adamski, 1999; Dieuaide-Noubhani et al.,
1997). Several other enzymes of the steroid metabolism
like 3 h-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase or 17-alpha-hydrox-
ylase have been described to be targets of the humoral
autoimmune response. Autoantibodies against those
enzymes have been found in some patients with Addison’s
disease (Krohn et al., 1992; Winqvist et al., 1992) , prema-
ture ovarian failure (Arif et al., 1996; Reimand et al., 2000) ,
autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome (Uibo et al., 1994;
Winqvist et al., 1993) and insulin-dependent diabetes (Arif
et al., 1996) . SMS is frequently associated with other
autoimmune disorders of the endocrine system like insu-
lin-dependent diabetes or polyendocrine autoimmune syn-
drome. The patient from which CB11 was derived had
antibodies to thyroid microsomal antigen and developed
insulin-dependent diabetes secondary to diagnosis of SMS.
We are not aware of a human disease that involves 17 h-
HSD4 or other peroxisomal enzymes as an autoimmune
target, and one can only speculate about possible effects of
anti-17h-HSD4 antibodies in serum or CSF. In humans,

several disorders are known that are caused by a severe
genetic defect of one or more peroxisomal enzymes (Moser
and Moser, 1996; Watkins et al., 1989; Wilson et al., 1986) .
Patients show a variety of symptoms like neonatal seizures,
neuronal migration defects or retinopathies (Kaufmann et
al., 1996) and die between the age of 9 months and 4 years.
Obviously, these diseases are hardly comparable to an
autoimmune reaction against a peroxisomal enzyme like
17h-HSD4, as they result from a gene defect already present
in embryonic development leading to neuronal heterotopias
and early death. However, considering the crucial impor-
tance of peroxisomal functions described for the nervous
system (Akaboshi et al., 1997; Moeller et al., 2001; van
Grunsven et al., 1998) , a relevance of anti-17 h-HSD4 anti-
bodies in a neurological autoimmune disease like SMS does
not seem unlikely.
In summary, a subgroup of SMS patients is characterized
by the appearance of 17 h-HSD4 antibodies supporting the
hypothesis that many different facultative symptoms seen in
individual SMS patients may occur on a heterogeneous
autoantibody background. Further studies will be required
to further establish etiology and relevance of anti-17 h-
HSD4 autoantibodies in SMS patients compared to patients
with other autoimmune diseases.

segments.text:
Abstract
Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) is a rare autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system associated with autoantibodies to glutamate
decarboxylase (GAD). We isolated five brain-reactive human monoclonal antibodies, with reactivity distinct from GAD, from peripheral
blood of a patient newly diagnosed with SMS. Two antibodies reacted with both Purkinje cells and ependymal cells, and precipitated an 80-
kDa protein from rat neuronal primary cultures, which was also recognized by 12% (3/25) of SMS sera and 13% (2/15) of SMS cerebrospinal
fluid (CSF) samples. The corresponding antigen was identified as 17 h-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 4 and may represent a possible
novel target of autoimmunity in SMS.
